item.title: Banned Nvidia Blackwell AI racks surface in China — data center tied to $14M loan and alleged spy Alice Huang
item.description:
A data center in Shanghai, China, is now running Nvidia's high-end Blackwell AI chips despite them being export-controlled and only available to whitelisted companies. Bloomberg reports that two Chinese companies installed the chips, including a GB300 NVL72 rack , which is among Nvidia's most capable products. The hardware was reportedly installed as collateral for a 96 million yuan ($14 million) loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank. The second firm, Shanghai Kezhan, installed a GB200 server, which also uses Nvidia's Blackwell silicon. The hardware was uncovered in documents related to a 90 million yuan loan in late 2025 from a finance-leasing firm wholly owned by a local Shanghai government agency.

The data center is linked to Alice Huang , a former Megaspeed employee, a company that was previously an Nvidia customer before concerns were raised about its potential role in bypassing the same export controls that should have prevented Blackwell chips from being shipped to China.

Blackwell chips have never been available to China without official licenses first being obtained from U.S. officials. While it's unconfirmed that Alice Huang or Megaspeed were directly involved in bringing the Blackwell-powered hardware to China, the coincidence is notable. Megaspeed is currently under a criminal investigation over concerns about what it was doing with the chips it bought from Nvidia. In 2025, it was claimed that it had helped move around $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips into the country illegally.

It's also important to note that the data center in question, known as the Yangtze River Delta Project, was described as Megaspeed's largest data center in 2024 when speaking with investors. Megaspeed used a render of the facility and described it as being in a "specific area" facility in an unspecified country.

The story is further complicated by the fact that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with his namesake when resigning from the company earlier this month. U.S. intelligence officials have also suggested that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy , and now believe her husband is heavily involved with China's Ministry of State Security . Jensen Huang is now back in charge at Nvidia after a push by U.S. President Donald Trump , among others.

Megaspeed has since been placed on a U.S. trade blacklist , though the U.S. still allows Nvidia and other companies to sell it lower-performance chips.

item.title: Caveman repurposes old mining rig for local AI, pools 72GB VRAM across mismatched GPUs — PCIe x1 slot hits just 10% load while running a 120B model
item.description:
Given that GPUs with any sizable amount of VRAM or horsepower are now made of unobtainium, enthusiasts looking to run LLMs locally try all sorts of tricks to use larger models. True to their moniker, X user Caveman Tech combined wildly different cards in the same rig, but not in the usual manner. They brought back a forgotten relic: a mining rig with PCIe x1 slots. Much to their surprise, the setup worked far better than it had any right to.

For their first trick, Tech used a Quadro RTX 4000 all on its own on the PCIe x1 slot, as opposed to the standard x16 connector. Running Qwen3-8B yielded the same 56 tokens/s output speed as before, with the only drawback being a longer model load at eight seconds — but unless you're running several models, you'll want to keep it in VRAM anyway. A number of software and hardware tweaks yielded even better results, upping tok/s to 96.

This result alone is contrary to the general zeitgeist that says low-bandwidth slots are not useful for AI work. Much like many comments, you're probably thinking that while the setup is serviceable, the true test comes when using multiple GPUs at once that need to talk to each other, so Caveman Tech obliged.

The second setup involved three cards in what can be described as a staggeringly asymmetric configuration: a CMP 170HX with 64 GB of VRAM on the primary PCIe x16 slot, the aforementioned Quadro 4000 (8 GB) on x1. The chosen model was now GPT-OSS-120B, and the pooled VRAM totaled 72 GB.

As a slap back to the naysayers, this configuration held up surprisingly well, as it turns out that with layer splitting (wherein the harness splits the model's layers across several GPUs), even the PCIe x1 link was only 10% busy. In this setup, cards only transmit the calculation results between them, not model weights.

The overall token generation speed dropped from 121 tok/s to 91 tok/s, likely due to the raw performance difference between the 170HX and the other two cards. As a point of comparison, letting the model spill to system RAM yielded only 52 token/s, less than half the original speed.

Caveman Tech did try an aggressive configuration in tensor mode, wherein all cards handle a portion of all layers, and only weights and the KV cache are split between them. That did bump the output to 101 tok/s, but prompt reading fell from the original 1,113 tok/s to 671, with the PCIe link 45% busy.

The conclusions are useful and straightforward: with judicious configuration, adding a card on a x1 link on a cheap mining rig is a perfectly reasonable way to expand the available VRAM, letting one use larger, smarter models that would be otherwise slow or downright impractical to run if they had to resort to system memory. It'd be interesting to see experiments with more than one GPU on x1 slots, as in theory the same conclusion should still hold.

item.title: FCC approves Elon Musk’s 1-million-satellite 'Starmind' orbital data center plan — first 747-sized compute unit due by 2033 despite Kessler Syndrome fears
item.description:
Elon Musk’s dream of putting AI data centers in space is moving forward as SpaceX’s proposal received approval from the Federal Communications Commission (FCC). According to The Wall Street Journal , the FCC approval gives the company until 2033 to launch the first data center satellite and until 2040 to launch the complete 1-million-strong constellation.

“America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence,” FCC chairperson Brendan Carr said in a statement. He also added, “The FCC supercharges that effort today by granting, for the first time ever, authorization to deploy 1 million orbital compute modules for data centers in space… This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home.”

SpaceX sought approval for its orbiting data center project , dubbed Starmind, in February 2026, with the company aiming to turn humanity into a Kardashev II-level civilization, which directly harvests energy from its nearby star. However, other companies like Amazon , satellite operator Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society objected to the proposal. Amazon said that SpaceX did not provide details about its deployment plan and the design of its satellites, while the American Astronomical Society feared that the increasing number of satellites orbiting the planet would disrupt Earth-bound astronomical observation and research.

Aside from those concerns, there’s also the possibility that having that many satellites orbiting the planet increases our risk of Kessler Syndrome. This is where orbiting debris would collide with a satellite, causing it to break up and introduce more debris. This could then lead to more collisions in space, leading to a chain reaction that could trap humanity on Earth for decades, if not centuries.

Despite this, Elon Musk is keen to get the project off the ground, especially as data centers on the ground face increasing opposition , like SpaceX’s campuses located near the border of Mississippi and Tennessee. The billionaire has already unveiled the design of its first compute satellite , AI1, which has a 120kW compute payload and spans wider than a Boeing 747, while the development of SpaceX’s massive Starship, which will be used to launch the satellites, continues at a fast pace.

Other companies and countries are also joining in the race to put data centers in orbit. Intel proposed two-tier low-earth orbit (LEO) data center satellites in August, while China put its own Supercomputing-1 satellite into orbit in September. Google ’s Project Suncatcher also launched a test orbital data center packed with four TPUs and 1,000 watts of solar power in October, even as another startup called Starcloud is targeting to launch its second spacecraft in 2027 after saying that it will be “the first to mine Bitcoin in space .”

item.title: AI enthusiast deletes Linux for a 24KB pure assembly OS that boots in 74 milliseconds — bare-metal Qwen3 setup is 28,000 times smaller than standard model, runs up to 54% faster than llama.cpp
item.description:
An intrepid developer has deleted their Linux OS and coded a tiny assembly language bare-metal bootable alternative to run LLMs. The result is a super-fast standalone system that starts in milliseconds and runs LLMs up to 54% faster. Moreover, Alexey Fateev, AKA alesha-pro on GitHub, has shared his Bare-Metal Bootable Qwen3-0.6B OS in 24 KB of Pure Assembly for other enthusiasts to code-tweak and test.

The compact size of this Multiboot OS binary (asm-llm-os.elf) is remarkable. Weighing in at just 24KB (24,252 bytes), it makes modern operating systems seem gargantuan. However, one must remember that the legendary Commodore 64 worked off a smaller 20KB ROM, which included not only the kernel but also a BASIC interpreter and a character generator.

Fateev says that his Multiboot OS with modern SMP support was written from scratch without Linux, Windows, C, Rust, or libc. Users interact with the new OS via its support for 80x25 character color VGA displays, PS/2 keyboards , and serial communications. Such is the purposeful efficiency of this hand-written NASM assembly language project that it can boot in 74-94 milliseconds directly to its multi-turn chat interface. You're ready to chat with your LLM in the blink of an eye.

While the OS and its carefully honed UI use only a tiny portion of the computer's resources, the OS loads Qwen3-0.6B Q8_0, which weighs in at 649MB. That's something of a lightweight LLM, as many of you will be aware, but it is roughly 28,000 times bigger than the OS that references it. That's good, as you bought your computer to run applications and games – not for running an OS – didn't you?

Turning to performance, this is another area where Fateev's standalone asm-llm-os.elf excels. In some head-to-head benchmarks of the compact new OS vs. the previous Linux install running the same LLM via llama.cpp, the pure assembly-coded OS was up to 54% faster. On the dev's AMD EPYC 7642 system, "4 threads hit 78.89 tok/s vs 51.08 (+54%)." That is the best result, and therefore highlighted, but is not a crazy outlier figure, with even the most modest performance uplift charted at +31% (when using 16 threads).

If you are interested in testing this project, Fateev has shared the full MIT source, ISO builder, and a setup guide at github.com/alesha-pro/llm.asm . Also, if bare-metal operation isn't required, you can test out the Linux-hosted version, which delivers the same basic asm-llm inference binary in just 14KB. That's because 10KB can be saved by removing the code required to boot the system, initialize the processor , keyboard, and monitor I/O, etc.

item.title: China’s AI hardware push is moving beyond GPUs to the PCBs underneath them — Beijing races to corner the market on copper foil and micro-drill bits as board complexity explodes
item.description:
Much of the attention on China's AI hardware industry has been focused on the country’s drive to develop domestic GPUs, including Huawei's Ascend processors , as U.S. export restrictions make it harder to buy advanced chips in the region. But making an AI server involves far more than securing its processors. The printed circuit boards (PCBs) connecting chips, memory, and networking equipment are becoming harder to manufacture, and Chinese companies are racing to supply the materials and equipment they require.

More than 20 Chinese PCB manufacturers announced major expansion plans in the first half of 2026. Three recent reports from HSBC and J.P. Morgan suggest the shortages could extend to products as unglamorous as drill bits and copper foil. Having a plentiful and regular supply of those components in the manufacturing process is important because the tiny drill bit used to make the circuit boards inside AI servers could be worn out after drilling fewer than 200 holes, according to HSBC, compared with around 2,000 holes for older materials.

It’s all part of a manufacturing process which stresses every part of the supply and manufacturing chain, beyond obvious components.

More holes, fewer uses

PCBs are built by layering copper and insulating material together, then drilling holes through them to connect their circuits. But the complexity of those boards is increasing as AI servers are designed to handle more data, including more layers than those seen in ordinary computers. HSBC estimates that a notebook PCB has four to eight layers, compared with more than 20 for Nvidia's H100 generation of GPUs.

But that’s just the beginning of the process. Analysts at the bank forecast that a backplane in Nvidia’s Rubin Ultra systems could contain 78 layers. Nor is the Rubin Ultra an outlier in that process: the bank also forecasts a 36% annual rise in the number of holes required per board between 2025 and 2028. The holes themselves are becoming more challenging to drill. According to a report by Taiwanese brokerage KGI Securities , the ratio between the depth of the hole and its diameter has increased from around 20:1 to 30:1 or 40:1. That requires pushing an extremely thin drill bit deeper into increasingly tough materials without bending or breaking it, or damaging the delicate circuitry, which can easily happen in such a sophisticated manufacturing process.

As well as the number of layers which have to be drilled through increasing in number, the materials involved are also adding complexity to the equation. New grades of copper-clad laminate — the glass-fibre-and-resin material onto which copper is bonded — are becoming trickier for the tiny tungsten-carbide tools previously used in the process to cut. “AI PCBs are denser with thicker layers, requiring more holes drilled per PCB,” writes Helen Fang, head of Asia Pacific industrials research at HSBC. The increasingly common use of harder laminates is resulting in the bits being consumed more quickly.

That’s good news for those making drill bits: HSBC forecasts global demand growing 55% a year in the coming three years. And as with many parts of the AI revolution, the voracious appetite of the sector means that supplies can’t keep up. Even with manufacturers increasing production, the bank forecasts a 24% supply shortfall in PCB drill bits in 2027.

That could push the world towards Chinese suppliers, right as the west is trying to wean itself off a dependency on the country for rare earths and other elements necessary to make GPUs. Guangdong Dtech, based in China, is the world’s largest PCB drill bit maker by volume. Around three in every 10 drill bits made in 2025 come from the company, with its monthly capacity potentially climbing from 160 million bits in June to more than 235 million by year-end. Japanese and Taiwanese manufacturers are still dominant at the premium end of the market, according to consultancy Frost & Sullivan, though Chinese manufacturers are trying to close that gap.

In its 2026 interim results , Dtech reported that it had begun mass-producing drill bits with aspect ratios exceeding 40:1, while developing techniques for producing bits exceeding 60:1. Its newer diamond-coated tools for particularly tough M9+ board materials have also entered small-scale use.

China calling

It’s not just in drill bits that China has a chokehold. Another Chinese manufacturer, Defu Technology, has historically been a key supplier of copper foil for lithium-ion batteries, but is increasingly changing its manufacturing processes to try and capitalise on the AI boom. “AI server PCB/CCL upgrades require smoother HVLP copper foil to reduce high-speed signal loss,” writes Avery Chan, a JP Morgan analyst.

HVLP stands for hyper-very-low-profile copper foil, and its manufacturers must make the surface smooth enough to minimise signal loss while making sure it can still stick to the insulating material it is attached to.

The business has historically been dominated by suppliers outside mainland China, with Japan’s Mitsui Kinzoku and Furukawa Electric, and Taiwan’s Co-Tech, holding more than 60% of global HVLP supply in 2025. Defu is trying to break in to disrupt that, with the firm shipping around 700 tonnes of HVLP foil in September, including more than 180 tonnes of HVLP4. JP Morgan’s Chan forecasts a shortage of qualified HVLP4 supply of around 700 tonnes a month in 2026, rising to 1,200 tonnes in 2027. Defu plans to add 50,000 tonnes of annual high-end PCB foil capacity over 2027 and 2028. But all the foil it creates will have to get past stringent testing.

Testing chips

Even before finished chips reach a server, they must be tested using specialist probe cards and sockets, which themselves rely on sophisticated PCBs of a type not found in a server but just used to check whether the chips work. “PCB is becoming the bottleneck and the value-add in probe cards,” wrote JP Morgan analyst Jerry Tsai.

Because of that, China is focusing attention there, too. In September, its Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and National Development and Reform Commission published a five-year plan calling for advances in high-frequency, high-speed and densely layered PCBs, alongside copper-clad laminates, low-profile copper foil and specialist manufacturing equipment.

But China won’t see the benefits of building new factories immediately. Producing the most sophisticated PCBs requires experience, specialist equipment and the ability to manufacture complex designs consistently at scale. Tsai warned that “the learning curve is measured in years, rather than quarters.”

item.title: Beijing’s AI ambitions are under threat as models may fall behind by up to nine months versus competitors — Chinese AI labs are under heavy fire from export controls, maturing chip stacks and a distillation crackdown
item.description:
This week, several reports have detailed how closing GPU rental loopholes across Asia may have had an impact on the development of Chinese AI models. In September, Mozilla estimated that open-weight AI models were three to six months behind the frontier. Since then, developments in the AI industry and export control rules could mean that Chinese AI models, many of which are typically open-weight, might fall even further behind Western counterparts, by up to nine months.

Zhipu AI, the developer of the GLM series of models, has allegedly pushed its release calendar back as a result of reduced access to advanced AI accelerators, Reuters said. It's an open secret that data centers located in Asia have been renting compute capacity to Chinese entities for some time . In light of the recent Nvidia scandal involving Jensen Huang and Megaspeed, the U.S. Department of Commerce has since tightened its rules over how data centers lend their compute capacity to Chinese entities. This has created an environment where there is, in fact, an excess of compute capacity available in the region, Bloomberg reported.

These curbs have a knock-on effect on how companies train their AI models, with Nvidia's AI accelerators being the most coveted; not having access to them stifles the development of AI in the region. However, this isn't entirely true across the industry. DeepSeek is attempting to wean itself off foreign silicon and instead adopting Huawei's Ascend AI chips , and porting its libraries away from CUDA and onto the open-source CANN. However, this hasn't stopped Chinese AI labs from facing another issue: tightened security against the distillation of AI models.

Distillation is a practice wherein the way a model thinks can be extracted and then learned from. It is largely believed to be the method in which Chinese AI labs have made great leaps in intelligence over the past several years, though several of China's leading labs refute that claim. The Western frontier has become more obtuse: Anthropic in October detailed how it's leveled up its own defences against distillation attacks, and the obfuscation of an AI model's chain of thought adds another hurdle. According to The Information , this is an issue that DeepSeek is now reportedly reckoning with. If distillation curbs the development of Chinese AI models even further, the gap between Eastern and Western frontier intelligence grows from three to six months to an estimated nine months.

The current standings

If you look at Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, which ranks AI models across a wide range of benchmarks and scores them in numerical order, Anthropic currently has the leading public AI model: Claude Fable 5.2, at a total of 65 points. Meanwhile, the leading Chinese AI model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, sits at 47. Between the two contenders are practically every Western frontier lab: OpenAI, Google , and Meta are all outgunning Chinese competitors, which were, just a few short months ago, competing at the frontier across many tasks.

It's important to mention that Artificial Analysis also changed its methodology over recent weeks, with China's AI models falling slightly further behind in added benchmarks, such as the Omniscience score, which tracks how often an AI is likely to hallucinate. This is paired with a jump in capability among the Western labs: Right now, it's on the Chinese AI labs' shoulders to respond in kind, and if current releases are anything to go by, they are falling short of expectations, especially in domains such as cybersecurity. An Epoch AI report characterized the difference in capabilities between GLM 5.3 and Claude Opus 5.5 as a six-to-seven-month gap in intelligence. With the release of newer models like Claude Fable 5.2, it's likely that gap has only widened, and the same story is likely to play out over the next few months across additional domains.

With additional safeguards against distillation and powerful compute resources becoming more difficult to find, this poses a difficult question for the Chinese labs: How can they keep up the pace and stay competitive while the odds are stacked against them?

China still holds the overall top spot in the open-weight arena with Kimi K3.1 Pro, though Western companies are bringing more performant models out as the months pass. China's second tier of open-weight models, which can often be run locally, e.g Alibaba's Qwen 3.8-27B (20 on AA), is facing competition from the American-made Thinking Machines Labs' Inkling 2 Mini (20 on AA), which was recently released. With the release of the larger (closed-weight and API only) Qwen 4 model seemingly not landing quite as well with users, it remains to be seen whether Alibaba can maintain the advantage of time, as Inkling 2 Mini was released just this week, while Qwen 3.8-27B has been out for several months.

With devices like the RTX Spark , AMD's AI Halo , and more, users are increasingly getting their own choice of running an open-weight AI, and for all intents and purposes, that usually means using a Chinese model to get the most intelligence out of your machine. However, recent developments show that smaller Western labs are also beginning to bridge that gap.

This is yet another arena in which Chinese and Western labs will want to wrest control from one another. Notably, Google has not released another series of Gemma models following Gemma 4 back in April. If a fifth generation of Google's Gemma models arrives, they'd likely be close cousins to the Gemini Neon, Carbon, Argon, and Hydrogen family, though that remains speculation until Google confirms anything official.

The silicon transition

Against the backdrop of export controls and tightening restrictions on AI distillation, Chinese AI labs are in a tough spot, and all eyes are on frontier labs like Moonshot AI, Zhipu, Deepseek, Alibaba, and Xiaomi to see if they can scale the intelligence wall that their Western counterparts currently present. More compute for training resources may be an answer, but for comparison's sake, Huawei's upcoming Ascend 950DT accelerator offers 2 PFLOPS of FP4 compute and 1 PFLOPS of FP8, while an Nvidia Rubin R200 offers 50 PFLOPS in inference and 35 PFLOPS in dense workloads. In memory capacity and bandwidth, the Ascend 950DT can offer 144GB of HiZQ 2.0 with 4 TB/s of bandwidth across a 2 TB/s interconnect. Rubin, on the other hand, offers 288GB of HBM4, with bandwidth ranging from 19.2-22 TB/s, across an NvLink interconnect at 2.6 TB/s.

If China's AI ambitions are to compete with the West, its silicon needs to either scale so the country can produce more chips to outgun a Western AI deployment with sheer numbers, or it needs to develop more advanced accelerators, while also managing the CANN software stack. The chips are figuratively, and literally, stacked heavily against China. As the race to develop Artificial Intelligence marches on, the Department of Commerce's latest measures have undoubtedly made it incredibly difficult for the country to compete.

item.title: TSMC gives a sneap peak at AI Design Kit: Agentic AI with foundry expertise
item.description:
The semiconductor industry is in a paradoxical situation these days. On the one hand, AI drives demand for the leading-edge nodes from both established players and new entrants, with everyone trying to accelerate the development cycle. On the other hand, leading-edge nodes become more complex, which increases entry barriers and stretches design cycles. While the challenge seems to be insoluble, it looks like TSMC has found a solution.

At its 2026 Europe OIP Ecosystem Workshop in Munich, TSMC this week unveiled its AI Design Kit (ADK), a collection of process-specific technical information, implementation guidelines, and design methodologies that enables AI agents to automate and optimize chip development flows.

The ADK complements the foundry's traditional process design kits (PDKs) and enables AI agents to use TSMC's process-specific expertise, knowledge of electronic design automation (EDA) tools, and customers' proprietary design methodologies to automate physical implementation and optimization of chips. Ultimately, the initiative aims to reduce development cycles, improve design productivity, and simplify adoption of TSMC's advanced process technologies.

"The ADK complements our traditional PDK, and it brings in capabilities to augment the EDA and other design flows," said Aveek Sarkar, Head of Ecosystem and Alliance Management at TSMC. "Our goal with these agentic flows is to bring in the technology-specific learning we have at TSMC and layer that with your orchestration layer, with your design expertise, and to support the next generation of EDA or design flows and methodologies that you have."

Why AI?

While every new fabrication process from TSMC offers advantages in terms of power, performance, and area (PPA), it also considerably increases design complexity. Compared to TSMC's N5-derived manufacturing technologies (including various N4 nodes), the number of design rules has increased by 2.3X with N3P, 3.1X with N2P, and 3.6X with A14 (the first node to be supported by the ADK).

Meanwhile, the number of available standard library cells has increased by 2.8X, 5X, and 4.6X, respectively. Add to that a greater number of metallization stack options and plenty of EDA tool settings, and the number of possible design configurations becomes massive. As a result, conventional design optimization methodologies approach their productivity limits, according to TSMC. At the same time, some of TSMC's customers want to reduce their chip development cycles from 18 months to 12 months, Sarkar said.

Usage of agentic AI could help chip developers to explore more design configurations within shorter timeframes, achieve more favorable PPA results from advanced process technologies, and potentially improve manufacturability and yields by implementing more extensive physical design optimization. Furthermore, it could reduce the amount of engineering work required to adopt a new fabrication process for a new design.

"AI is bringing a significant benefit: faster design cycles, more verification coverage, faster time to closure," Sarkar said.

Do physical implementation faster

TSMC's early-phase AI Design Kit incorporates process-specific information, such as metal pitches, standard cell heights, routing track patterns, library cell naming conventions, and implementation guidelines, according to slides demonstrated at the event.

With the ADK, EDA agents — such as Cadence's InnoStack or Synopsys's Implementation Agent — can use a simple natural-language prompt and a large language model (LLM) to automatically generate a qualified automatic placement and routing (APR) reference flow for TSMC's A14 process technology. Such a flow includes project setup, library cell usage, placement and routing optimization, routing track and power grid creation, and wide-wire configuration. Traditionally, engineers could spend weeks on preparation of such scripts, but now APR scripts could be prepped with a natural language prompt, though TSMC did not disclose the actual time it takes to prep them (probably because it depends on design complexity and goals).

"Instead of spending weeks preparing APR scripts, EDA agents can take a simple prompt from users and the TSMC ADK and use a generative model to deliver a qualified APR reference flow," a spokesperson from TSMC said at the stage.

For more sophisticated design tasks, TSMC proposes an orchestration agent that resides at the customer's site and combines three sources of knowledge with clear ownership:

  • Proprietary in-house design know-how, constraints, guidelines, and customized flow;
  • Specialized EDA agents that know how to use EDA tools and their capabilities;
  • TSMC's ADK that provides design reference package and technology-specific information on top of what EDA agent and tools know.

The orchestrator coordinates agents responsible for design diagnostics, power grid implementation, timing closure, design rule checks, and congestion mitigation. These agents analyze EDA tool output and automatically adjust parameters for subsequent iterations across floorplanning, placement, clock tree synthesis, routing, sign-off, and engineering change orders (ECOs). Such a methodology enables continuous design optimization 24/7 with less human intervention.

"The orchestrator then directs these agents to analyze the output of EDA tools and automatically adjust the settings for the next iteration across floorplan, placement, CTS, routing, sign-off, and ECO," the spokesman said. "This agentic AI flow drives the iterative design process 24/7, minimizing the turnaround time and maximizing productivity."

Complement, not replace

For now, TSMC's ADK primarily addresses physical implementation rather than chip architecture or logic design. The company has not demonstrated an autonomous design flow that takes a chip from an architectural specification to tape-out without human intervention. Nor has TSMC disclosed quantified PPA improvements, actual reductions in development cycles, or a commercial availability timeframe for its ADK.

It is noteworthy that TSMC's ADK neither replaces conventional PDKs nor substitutes for advanced AI-enabled EDA software from Cadence, Synopsys, Siemens EDA, or other developers. Instead, it provides process-specific knowledge that enables AI agents to make more informed decisions, while the actual physical implementation, simulation, optimization, and verification tasks remain the domain of specialized EDA tools. Thus, chip developers cannot use the ADK independently of traditional EDA infrastructure.

Strategic importance

For TSMC, the ADK could accelerate adoption of its latest fabrication processes, as customers could adapt their design methodologies to new nodes faster. Smaller fabless chip developers could also gain access to sophisticated physical design methodologies without the need to develop expertise comparable to that of prominent chip developers entirely in-house. Meanwhile, EDA and IP providers could benefit from closer integration of their products into process-specific design flows, whereas contract chip designers could offer shorter development times for their customers without significant additional investments.

There is also a potential customer lock-in aspect. While TSMC's proposed architecture preserves customers' ownership of proprietary design knowledge, extensive integration of foundry-specific physical design enablement collateral, EDA agents, and internal orchestration systems could make migration to another foundry harder and generally less likely as chipmakers get more accustomed to TSMC ADK (which is an exclusive capability for now and will remain an exclusive offering for a while). In effect, TSMC's competitive advantages will extend well beyond its process technologies, production capabilities, and conventional design ecosystem to include intelligence that emphasizes its customers' chip development methodologies.

item.title: AMD and Winbond vulnerabilities let attackers brute-force BitLocker PINs on millions of PCs — cracking a six-digit PIN drops from 19 years to 20 days
item.description:
Former owners of laptops gained yet another concern today. Firmware-backed drive encryption setups like Windows' BitLocker are meant to protect against someone stealing your laptop or desktop computer. Prospective thieves would have a hard time guessing your PIN, as they'll eventually have to wait 10 minutes for each attempt. That is, unless your machine uses a modern AMD CPU or relies on Winbond's SPI flash — in which case your data may be open for inspection in a few days, or even hours, as researchers from Technische Universität Berlin found out .

The paper covers many vulnerabilities, but we'll focus on the big three. All focus on having a way to brute-force an encrypted drive's password in a matter of days/hours rather than years. Physical access is required for the attacks, but hardware theft is precisely the scenario that disk encryption is meant to protect against.

An attacker makes brute-forcing easier by resetting, or pretending to increase, the counter that records the number of failed unlock attempts. On Intel- and AMD-based PCs using the fTPM for security — nearly all modern x86 consumer machines — this counter is stored encrypted in an SPI flash chip on the motherboard.

Standard procedure is to allow for 32 attempts in succession, then force the machine to wait 10 minutes for each additional one, resulting in many years for unlocking a short PIN — 19 years for a six-digit numerical PIN, under normal conditions. We should note the attacks likely extend to other fTPM-based disk encryption mechanisms, not just BitLocker. While encryption keys can be alphanumeric, Microsoft Windows does default to using a numeric PIN for sign-in, and most users don't use long ones.

First up: machines based on Winbond's RPMC-enabled SPI flash (variant with rollback protection), used by many OEMs across both Intel and AMD platforms. Although it's hard to pin down the number of affected machines, the paper claims Winbond has roughly a 25% market share for SPI flash — so, potentially millions of machines. With a simple voltage glitch, the researchers made the chip reveal the HMAC key, the datum that signs commands when the TPM and the SPI chip talk to each other.

With the HMAC in hand, the thief places a low-cost interposer board in front of the SPI chip to impersonate it. On a failed unlock, the computer will request a counter increase and get a confirmation, when in reality nothing happened — allowing for repeat attempts as fast as Windows lets them, at five per reboot. There is no fix for this vulnerability other than replacing the SPI chip with one that doesn't contain the bug.

The team glitched two specific Winbond chip models, but they theorize the issue extends further into the maker's lineup, as the flaw allegedly lies with the RPMC engine design. Flash chips from other firms in the test were not affected to the same extent.

As for AMD machines, the situation is both worse and better, with two related vulnerabilities. The team verified at least one of the two attacks across AMD machines from Zen 2 up to an AI 5 330 laptop. They theorize that considering the mechanisms, all contemporary AMD setups may be vulnerable, at least for standard consumer hardware using fTPM. That's multiple millions of machines potentially at risk, on the low side.

The first is simple enough. On the tested machines whose SPI flash didn't use RPMC — rollback protection — you can just make a copy of the SPI flash's contents when the counter is low, and just flash it again once you've used up your free tries. Bad enough, yes, but the second vulnerability should elicit facepalms from security architects.

According to the paper, AMD's firmware controller for non-volatile storage — the bit that talks to the SPI flash — does not verify that the failed-attempt counter increase actually took place. It'll just issue the order to +1 it and be done, opening the avenue for an attacker to simply intercept that order (again, with a cheap board) and ignore it without even needing HMAC keys, so the counter never changes.

The latter vulnerability should be fixable via a firmware update, almost certainly via AMD's AGESA software. The problem is one of practicality: in the past, updating AGESA on client hardware meant that every OEM had to create fresh BIOSes for affected machines, many of which are assuredly out of their support window.

Anyone who's lived through the Spectre and Meltdown days knows how hard it is in practice, as OEMs are exceedingly slow to publish updates, and have a distaste for providing fixes for hardware that's more than a few years old.

The researchers contacted every company involved in their tests, informing them of their findings, but sadly "none of them has committed to fixing the root-cause vulnerabilities" — at least, as of this writing, only Microsoft announced a policy change recommending users enter six-digit PINs instead of the current four during setup.

item.title: Kioxia's 3rd-gen XL-Flash hits Optane-class 3-microsecond read latency with 70% higher density — samples March 2027 ahead of 18-million-IOPS GP2 SSDs
item.description:
The Kioxia Corporation showcased a prototype of its new XL-Flash Generation 3 technology, next-generation low-latency, high-performance flash memory, at its KIOXIA Forum in Tokyo. The flash, which uses CMOS directly Bonded to Array, or CBA, for better power efficiency and storage density, is about 135% more efficient with 70% higher bit density than Gen 2, and its 3 µs average read latency is less than 10% of that of Kioxia’s standard BiCS8 TLC. Samples are due March 2027, and Kioxia named its GP2 enterprise SSDs, rated for more than 18 million 512-byte random read IOPS, as its first product using it.

The low-latency XL-Flash fills “a new memory tier” to bridge the gap between DRAM and regular flash memory, in a way that can complement or replace some DRAM to help drive down costs, especially in AI servers and data centers. This has some similarities to Optane , which used 3D XPoint instead, as a storage class memory (SCM) option to reach higher IOPS. Intel and Micron’s 3D XPoint stored bits as changes in the cell material’s resistance rather than as trapped charge like NAND, and Intel exited the Optane business in 2022. The XL-Flash NAND is built on BiCS flash technology, but it’s tuned for low read latency and high write endurance.

The first generation was SLC with under-5 µs reads, arriving in 2019. By 2022, Gen 2 added 2-bit MLC as an option for lower bit cost, trading some like-for-like performance for better price-to-density. Gen 3 is reported to use SLC, and its 3 µs average read latency challenges the first gen’s sub-5 µs rating while being more than ten times faster than the 40 µs of standard BiCS8 TLC. This is within the same ballpark as Optane SSDs. The flash also reportedly has SLC endurance at 150,000 to 250,000 P/E cycles, at least 50x standard TLC, running at a 4.8 Gb/s interface speed.

XL-Flash achieves lower latency, in part, by using more, smaller planes (16 per die, with a 4KB page, on earlier generations), which is common with SLC and low-latency flash, and especially helps with smaller I/O. Kioxia’s GP drives target 512B accesses rather than the typical 4KB, a pattern that matches developments in enterprise storage requirements for AI and other emerging workloads that involve constant fine-grained memory lookups. 3D XPoint would outmatch it for write performance, though, due to not needing to erase for new data.

The newer gen is able to maintain high levels of performance at much higher density thanks to CBA bonding, where Kioxia makes the logic CMOS wafer and flash memory-cell wafer separately and later bonds them. This technology also improves the efficiency of 512-byte reads, by Kioxia’s own tests, which matches the design intention of the forthcoming GP2. Kioxia hasn’t disclosed full details on the flash, such as layer count.

The GP2 Super High IOPS SSD will be Kioxia’s first product to use the new flash, promising high levels of performance, including up to 28 GB/s sequential reads, if it can saturate PCIe 6.0 x4 as expected. Kioxia’s 2.5x IOPS number, versus “typical TLC-based SSDs,” comes from a comparison to its own CM10 drives, for 512B I/O . Endurance will also be excellent at up to 50 drive writes per day, which is within the ballpark of Optane storage.

Kioxia is considering E1.S and E3.S form factors, and the drive will support direct liquid cooling, which is increasingly necessary for certain data centers, including GPU-heavy ones where the GP2 is likely to operate.

These drives will serve as a flash tier to help get more out of a GPU’s HBM, and Kioxia first showed the GP series with Nvidia earlier this year . Offloading memory by any means possible is becoming a strategy with AI, even at the enthusiast level , due to high memory demands and how the technology and its KV caching work.

While the flash should sample to select customers before the end of the first quarter of 2027, Kioxia only promises GP2 evaluation samples to select customers by the end of that year. Exact specifications for the drive may differ, but what is clear is that later GP drives will target up to 100 million random-read IOPS that Kioxia and Nvidia have been working toward for AI servers. Kioxia announced its XL1 series of CXL memory expansion modules on XL-Flash in August, and it “will continue to leverage the speed, power efficiency, and endurance of XL-FLASH” for emerging data center needs.

item.title: Nvidia agrees to $290 million settlement over 2018 crypto mining GPU sales — ends eight-year investor lawsuit without admitting wrongdoing
item.description:
Nvidia has agreed to pay a $290 million settlement in an eight-year-long securities class action lawsuit. Investors accused the company of misleading shareholders about how much of its gaming revenue was actually driven by the cryptocurrency mining boom in 2018.

2017-2018 were some of the most rampant years for cryptocurrency mining, with plenty of scalpers buying up the Pascal GTX 1000-Series GPUs released in early 2017. Nvidia also sold the P106-100 that year, a dedicated cryptocurrency mining GPU with similar hardware to the GTX 1060, and it was attributed to OEM sales. Many gamers remember how scarce retail gaming GPUs were in those years, yet Huang stated in November 2017 that what cryptocurrency contributes is “small but not zero,” as highlighted in the Summary of Alleged False and Misleading Statements section of the March court filing .

When the 2018 crypto crash hit, Nvidia’s revenue felt it too, with a sharp decline in gaming sales. The plaintiffs saw this strong correlation, seeing how cryptocurrency demand closely followed gaming GPU sales. The litigation states that Nvidia was “forced to partially reveal the truth on August 16, 2018, when it lowered their revenue guidance and acknowledged that ‘a great deal’ of cryptocurrency miners had bought GeForce Gaming GPUs.” Following the admissions, Nvidia’s stock price also fell 28.5% over two trading sessions.

After the crash, Nvidia struggled with excess inventory, with CFO Colette Kress stating that “Gaming was short of expectations as post-crypto channel inventory took longer than expected to sell through,” painting a clearer picture of how much crypto impacted Nvidia’s sales, which were allegedly attributed to gaming sales. It’s unclear how much of those gaming sales were from cryptocurrency mining, but considering that an overwhelming amount of retail gaming GPUs were bought out by cryptocurrency miners, it’s reasonable to say it’s difficult to keep track of who purchased and for what purpose.

In 2021, the district court dismissed the lawsuit, but part of the dismissal was reversed by the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, reviving the lawsuit and allowing the securities fraud claims against Nvidia to proceed. Nvidia still denies wrongdoing, but has decided to settle, agreeing with the plaintiffs to pay $290 million in September, according to the Tuesday court filing .

item.title: Texas lifts freeze on 1,800+ data center projects in Greg Abbott U-turn — companies rush for permits before Gina Hinojosa's January arrival
item.description:
After slamming the brakes on more than 1,800 data center projects in August, Texas has once again started approving them following a new directive from outgoing Republican governor Greg Abbott's office. The move came after the same office also paused the approval of permits, saying that Abbot's "top priority is to protect Texans’ safety and quality of life” amid concerns over the amount of power new data centers would require. At the time, the move meant that 474 gigawatts of new power requests became subject to the moratorium. But with Democratic governor Gina Hinojosa's January arrival edging ever closer, Abbott has done a 180-degree pivot, with the FT reporting that data center builders are rushing to get their approvals in before the new governor arrives. Hinojosa has already pledged to rein in new data center construction.

As recently as October, Texas suspended a further 17 data center construction permits and shut down an automated portal that was found to still be approving new permits. That system will surely be switched back on now that Abbott's office has confirmed that the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), which is in charge of the state’s electrical grid, has finished gathering the information that it needed on how data centers affect local communities.

But even with ERCOT's investigation complete, the processing of new power requests isn't one that is expected to happen quickly. With that in mind, some developers have already taken matters into their own hands, choosing to build their own power centers to reduce or eliminate their reliance on the local grid. item.title: Activists enter third day of hunger strike outside Anthropic's San Francisco HQ over recursive AI self-improvement — protester threatens to go 40+ days and target OpenAI next
item.description:
The AI market and its developments have continually garnered opposition from several areas of society, to the point where protests are now frequent. On the day of Anthropic's IPO, Nov. 19, there were protests in multiple locations . As of right now, there's a fellow by the name of Elliot Callender on his third day of hunger strike in front of Anthropic's San Francisco offices, protesting against the company's use of RSI, or AI Recursive Self-Improvement.

For now, he seems gung-ho about the effectiveness of his hunger strike, remarking that "It would be bad press for Anthropic if I had to go 40+ days to pressure them," and noted that he intends to protest with OpenAI once he's done with Anthropic. He also urges California residents to ring up Governor Gavin Newsom and request a legislative session on the topic of RSI.

Callender just had a fellow protester join him now, too, though they might have a hard road ahead changing the hearts of CEOs who believe your ownership of RAM is a bad thing , and that immersive video games would be excellent entertainment for those unemployed due to AI.

RSI is an AI training method wherein a model is put to work to improve itself repeatedly in a test-feedback-improve loop, purportedly making for much faster evolution compared to normal methods. It's a safe bet that most every frontier lab is using it, and Anthropic in particular has said that Claude wrote 90% of its own code back in September.

Many AI opponents consider that the field is moving too fast , for several reasons. The first claim is that there's not enough time or oversight to ensure the proper testing and safety of the developed models. Others consider that the economic impact is too violent and coming in too fast and would broadly prefer a slowdown. Some also consider that reaching some sort of general intelligence (AGI) is feasible and see that as a doomsday scenario best left to cinematic productions.

Proponents of RSI broadly coalesce around the fact that if one lab, or a nation's labs, stop using RSI, then someone else inevitably will — particularly but not only from nations with questionable human rights track records. The protesters' counter-argument is that countries need AI cooperation treaties, a point that Callender subscribes to: "they should stop doing RSI, put all of their money into lobbying for a bilateral AI treaty, and directly warn their users about their product."

Such treaties are viewed with skepticism at best, considering how physically invisible model training is, requiring just data centers with the appropriate hardware. If the current U.S.-China-Nvidia situation surrounding high-end AI accelerators is any illustration, it's arguable if there's truly any international interest in controlling frontier AI development to begin with, much less choosing how quickly it's performed.

This massive shortage has pushed up costs for electronic manufacturers, with some companies forced to increase prices to make up the difference while others cut the specifications of their products while introducing a smaller price bump.

The Wall Street Journal reports that Taiwanese memory module and storage maker Apacer had to take out loans just to have money on hand in case it finds a supply of memory chips. “If chips show up, we take it,” Apacer President Gibson Chen told the publication. “This is crazy, but there is no other way.” Even one of the world’s richest people, Elon Musk, was reportedly having trouble finding memory chips. A portfolio manager claimed that Musk offered Samsung an LTA and even a financial guarantee for new Samsung chip factories, but the company’s executive chairman, Lee Jae-yong, allegedly answered that everyone else was offering those things already. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also recently went to South Korea to meet with Samsung leadership just to secure more RAM for data centers.

Even though PC builders and enthusiasts were the hardest hit by the 500% climb in memory prices , many other electronics manufacturers are also now feeling the squeeze. Big companies like Amazon , Apple, and Microsoft could use their scale and resources to pay more and secure massive amounts of memory chip supplies under long-term agreements (LTAs). However, smaller firms would usually have to rely on brokers and whatever’s available to find what they need. Some have reportedly contacted hundreds of brokers and go through online listings, where they would snap up even small batches of just five or 12 units just to have some supply. Others proceed to the gray market, although they must be careful as some unscrupulous sellers mix in batches of used memory chips with brand new orders to inflate their deliveries.

The scramble for AI compute has caused a massive memory chip shortage , especially as the big three memory chip manufacturers — Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix — have focused their production on more lucrative HBM. Both memory chip manufacturers and RAM kit makers are warning of continued shortages, too, with SK hynix saying 2027 will be the “worst year” for memory shortages , while TeamGroup’s CEO said that it could reach a point where “even money can’t buy goods.” Although the big three manufacturers are building new factories, they’re not expected to go online and start pushing out memory chips until 2028.

It’s difficult for a new player to enter the memory chip market. Aside from the enormous costs involved in setting up a factory and supply chain to build memory chips, any potential entrant must also license a ton of patents and develop its own technologies before it can start making competitive chips. Even if it was able to get its hands on the knowledge required to design memory chips, it still needs the manufacturing expertise needed to produce them at scale. CXMT is the only new player that has successfully produced mainstream consumer DDR5 RAM , but it’s facing multiple allegations that it stole the technology needed to achieve that from Samsung. Even then, the DDR5 memory chips that the Chinese company produced don’t have the same performance as its competitors and track market prices, meaning it’s not the affordable alternative that many tech enthusiasts imagined it to be.

The memory chip market is known for its boom-and-bust cycle, which is why manufacturers were initially reluctant to increase their capacity. But even if they started building factories at the first sign of a shortage, it would still take several years before these new facilities could start pumping out chips to ease the situation. Nevertheless, the three companies are currently facing a price-fixing lawsuit alleging that they coordinated their shift to HBM to cut DDR3 and DDR4 production, with the judge handling the case saying that it’s plausible they colluded as the market experienced the price surge.

item.title: Inside the indium phosphide squeeze and the optical boom — InP remains tightly constrained as the demand from AI puts the entire supply chain under pressure
item.description:
Indium phosphide (InP) is a compound material used in specialized chip-making. Unlike silicon, which is the fundamental building block for mainstream logic and memory chips, InP — made from indium and phosphorus — is mainly used to manufacture highly specialized photonic and high-frequency electronic chips, largely due to its outstanding optical properties. Its immensely expensive and complex manufacturing process also makes it impractical for the large volumes and die sizes needed for logic and memory chips. With the industry predicting a shortfall of this crucial material right as the shift to optical interconnects in data centers begins, we explore the current state of the supply chain.

InP chips have powered high-speed lasers, modulators, photodetectors, and various other optical components used across the telecommunications industry and defense for decades. While the InP supply chain was relatively small and highly specialized, it was generally stable and sufficient to meet global demands.

Then came the AI boom. As AI clusters hit the physical limits of moving enormous amounts of data over copper, the industry began the switch to optical interconnects. First came ever-faster optical transceivers. Now the industry is transitioning to silicon photonics , near-packaged optics, and co-packaged optics, bringing optical links progressively closer to the processors themselves. InP is central to much of this transition, building the critical active optical components needed to turn electrical data into light and back again.

Individual AI data centers are already being built around hundreds of thousands of accelerators, with upcoming gigawatt-scale buildouts expected to house millions . Connecting those processors translates into demand for millions upon millions of indispensable optical components, all relying on the same relatively tiny InP supply chain.

Japan's Sumitomo Electric and U.S.-headquartered AXT together account for almost 80% of global InP substrate manufacturing, with JX Advanced Metals adding roughly another 10%. AXT, however, manufactures most of its InP substrates in China, where exports now require government licenses, further exacerbating the situation. It gets worse: China accounts for around 70% of global refined indium output, which is recovered as a byproduct of processing zinc. Export controls mean that restrictions apply to both the material itself and the finished wafer.

The resulting squeeze is already sending ripples across the industry, with several companies predicting shortfalls. Michael Hurlston, CEO of optical-component manufacturer Lumentum, said in July that the company's InP fabs were shipping more than 30% below customer demand , despite rapid capacity expansion. Coherent also described InP capacity as the “primary constraint” on its transceiver business.

A simple solution would be to expand the supply chain. However, growing large, low-defect InP crystals is difficult, while qualifying new suppliers requires time that doesn't align with the industry's demand. Furthermore, expanding substrate and laser-fabrication capacity can take years. Meanwhile, to secure optical components capacity for its accelerators, Nvidia has invested $2 billion each in Lumentum and Coherent , attaching multibillion-dollar purchase commitments and future capacity rights to both deals. Both companies, along with several others in the supply chain, are frantically pursuing solutions.

What is indium phosphide?

Indium phosphide belongs to the III-V family of compound semiconductors, named after the periodic-table groups of their constituent elements; in InP’s case, indium and phosphorus. Its better-known relatives include gallium arsenide and gallium nitride.

Indium phosphide’s distinguishing property, which separates it from silicon, is its direct bandgap, measured at about 1.34 eV at room temperature. In a direct-bandgap material, electrons dropping across the gap release their energy efficiently as photons, making the material particularly useful for lasers and other active optical devices.

Silicon, on the other hand, has an indirect bandgap, meaning that the same transition requires an additional interaction with a crystal lattice and mostly sheds its energy as heat instead. Therefore, while the material can — in silicon photonics — guide, split, and modulate light using structures fabricated with mature CMOS processes, it does not produce the light beam. As a result, Modern silicon-photonics systems commonly rely on a III-V laser source, most commonly based on the InP material system, to provide the light that the silicon circuitry manipulates.

The fiber-optic wavelength window’s alignment with InP's properties is another reason for the material's ubiquity. Modern telecom and data-center links commonly operate around 1,310 nm and 1,550 nm, where optical fiber exhibits favorable transmission characteristics. Pure InP itself does not emit at those exact wavelengths. However, InGaAsP and InAlGaAs alloys, which are grown on lattice-matched InP substrates, can have their bandgaps engineered for those bands. InGaAs layers on InP are also highly effective photodetectors at telecom wavelengths.

These characteristics and functionalities make the InP platform critical to many active functions in optical communications, including distributed-feedback (DFB) lasers, electro-absorption modulated lasers (EMLs), continuous-wave (CW) lasers, semiconductor optical amplifiers, photodetectors, and complete photonic integrated circuits. Silicon photonics and InP consequently complement each other. Silicon provides scalable optical circuitry, while InP provides efficient light generation and several high-performance active optical devices.

Beyond photonics, InP is also commonly used in high-frequency electronic chips. Electrons move through the material far faster than through silicon, giving it strong high-frequency performance that makes it suitable for millimeter-wave and terahertz electronics, radar receivers, and high-speed data converters. This market is much smaller than photonics, but it has few substitutes at the top of the frequency range.

Indium phosphide’s roles across telecommunications and AI data centers

InP lasers and transceivers have been converting electrical signals into light for long-haul fiber networks, metro links, submarine cables, and eventually shorter-reach data-center connections for decades. Despite 5G rollouts driving demand higher, the indium phosphide supply chain remained a stable, moderately sized business with predictable growth. The AI boom has now driven demand up by several orders of magnitude.

Modern AI clusters can contain hundreds of thousands of interconnected accelerators that continuously exchange data. Copper remains a cheap, effective connector over short distances, but electrical losses, signal integrity, and power requirements progressively worsen as bandwidth and distance increase. This has led to the rapid adoption of optical interconnects .

In this setup, a modulator encodes electrical data from the switch or accelerator onto light from a laser. Fiber cables then carry it across the link to a photodetector that converts the received photons back into an electrical signal. In pluggable transceivers, many of these functions are integrated into a compact module plugged into the front of a network switch, with InP-based components executing several steps in the process.

Lumentum's 200G EML, for example, monolithically combines a wavelength-locked DFB laser and an electro-absorption modulator on its InP platform, and is designed for 200-Gbps-per-lane links used in 1.6T transceivers. Coherent is producing InP EMLs, high-power CW lasers, and high-speed photodiodes for the same generation of hardware. As aggregate link speeds move from 400G and 800G to 1.6T and beyond, the number and performance of these InP-based optical components become increasingly important.

At the same time, the industry is bringing optics right to the board with co-packaged optics (CPO) to further shorten the distance data travels. Conventional pluggable optics leave around 15 to 30 centimeters (5.90 to 11.81 inches) of high-speed copper trace between the switch ASIC and the optical module. CPO brings the optical engine onto the accelerator package as a photonic integrated circuit (PIC) chip, shrinking that electrical path and reducing power consumption. Nvidia's Quantum-X and Spectrum-X photonics switches are among the first major AI platforms built around that approach.

While they integrate several optical functions onto the boards, PIC chips do not generate the laser. CPO and silicon-photonics designs still mostly use external InP CW lasers to supply light to the silicon photonic circuits, further consolidating the demand for indium phosphide in AI data centers and the industry as a whole.

The state of the supply chain

As a result of the enormous, rapidly expanding market for the material, indium phosphide’s supply chain is constrained at several points, starting with the raw material itself. Unlike many metals which are mined from dedicated deposits, indium is typically recovered as a trace byproduct of processing zinc sulfide ore. Manufacturers then combine high-purity indium and phosphorus and grow them into a single-crystal InP ingot, or boule, which they process into substrate wafers with tightly controlled properties. Next, manufacturers grow extremely thin epitaxial layers of InP-related compounds over it, commonly using metal-organic chemical vapor deposition. The epiwafer then goes through several chip-making processes and module assembly to become optical chips and devices.

Indium production's dependence on Zinc processing creates bottlenecks in InP's supply chain, right at the beginning of the stream. The USGS put global primary refined indium production at roughly 1,100 tonnes in 2025, with China accounting for 760 tonnes. For context, the BBC estimates that 30,000 tonnes of electronic-grade silicon used exclusively to make microchips are mined yearly. The United States imports all of the InP it consumes, producing nothing. Meanwhile, indium substrate manufacturers Japan's Sumitomo and JX Metals source more than 90% of their high-purity indium feedstock from China, meaning even non-Chinese substrate makers begin their process with Chinese material.

Further downstream, at the substrate manufacturing level, Sumitomo Electric holds roughly 40% of the global InP substrate market, U.S.-based AXT around 35%, and JX Advanced Metals about 10%. Together, the three control more than 90% of capacity. Although AXT is headquartered in California, most of its InP substrate production runs through its Beijing Tongmei subsidiary, which puts it directly under China's export licensing regime. Other fringe substrate manufacturers include Freiberger Compound Materials in Germany and a growing set of Chinese entrants, including Yunnan Germanium.

The supply chain is also highly concentrated at the device and component level, with Coherent and Lumentum dominating Western laser and component production. IQE supplies epitaxial wafers, and Japanese firms, including Mitsubishi Electric, supply laser components. Chinese module makers such as Innolight and Eoptolink assemble a large share of the world's finished 800G modules, pairing Western lasers with Broadcom and Marvell DSPs. We recently explored how this entanglement complicates any attempt to decouple the two ecosystems, even as the FCC is considering a ban on Chinese optical hardware . Coherent primarily sources substrates from AXT, while Lumentum relies heavily on Sumitomo and JX.

On the technical side, wafer-size limitations in InP semiconductors add another constraint. While silicon logic and memory moved to 300-mm wafers in the early 2000s, the InP industry is only now transitioning from 3-inch to 6-inch (150-mm) production; primarily because the material is brittle, expensive, and grown in small boules, factors that limit wafer size. Doubling the wafer diameter gives four times the area. Coherent's six-inch line, for example, yields more than four times as many devices as its three-inch line at a lower cost per die. On the other hand, moving a fab to six-inch requires new crystal-growth recipes, new handling equipment, new process qualification, and extensive customer requalification.

The supply chain was already struggling under these constraints when, in February 2025, Beijing placed InP, trimethylindium, triethylindium, and the technology used to produce them under export controls , requiring licenses for overseas shipments. AXT called the export controls its most significant current challenge, noting that even with sufficient capacity and strong demand, its ability to ship outside China depends on Chinese licensing decisions.

The shortfall and the race to expand

The widening gap between demand and InP industry output points to a fast-approaching shortfall. Coherent first warned of an InP shortage on its May earnings call. At the close of its fiscal year in August, CEO Jim Anderson described indium phosphide availability as the company's primary constraint, confirming that transceiver assembly and test capacity were available.

Lumentum CEO Hurlston said in July that telecom customers historically ordered lasers in the hundreds, while Nvidia and the hyperscalers were asking for hundreds of millions. Despite operating multiple InP fabs, Lumentum was shipping more than 30% below customer requirements. Earlier in the year, Hurlston said the company's capacity was sold out through 2027 and probably into 2028, even with the expanded output. In both cases, capacity was mostly bought out via Nvidia’s $4 billion investment.

To ease the multifaceted bottleneck, the industry is pursuing several solutions simultaneously, primarily expansions. Coherent is expanding its Sherman, Texas campus, reportedly described as the first and largest high-volume 6-inch InP semiconductor manufacturing facility. Washington signed a letter of intent in June for up to $50 million in CHIPS Act funding for the expansion. Coherent is now on track to double internal InP output in 2026, one quarter ahead of its original plan, and more than double it again by the end of 2027, while also adding 6-inch production in Sweden and Zurich.

Lumentum, meanwhile, is converting a 240,000-square-foot former Qorvo gallium-arsenide facility in North Carolina, which it bought for about $18 million, into another InP fab. The relevance of these expansions largely depends on the downstream InP substrate supply. Lumentum signed an agreement in July to reserve AXT InP substrate capacity through 2031, with an initial $43.5 million deposit and another $43.5 million payment contemplated for 2028. Coherent signed its own three-year 6-inch supply agreement with AXT a month earlier and prepaid $22.3 million against committed capacity.

The substrate suppliers are also expanding in kind. AXT is channeling fresh funds into Beijing Tongmei to double capacity by the end of 2026 and double it again in 2027. Similarly, JX Advanced Metals plans to invest roughly ¥120 billion ($746 million) through FY2030 to lift capacity seven to ten times above FY2025 levels, its largest-ever commitment in semiconductor materials.

Indium production — the uppermost stage of the stream — is far less active, with the biggest hurdle being the reliance on Zinc production. Global zinc mine production hasn't grown materially since 2011, sitting at or below 13 million tonnes a year, according to analysts. Wood Mackenzie expects just 0.1% growth in 2026. On the other hand, not everyone expects the crunch to last. LightCounting estimated in April that optical component demand exceeded supply by about 30% but projected that shortages would largely clear by the end of 2026 as new capacity comes online.

There are also viable, albeit slow, technical workarounds to ease the crunch. Heterogeneous integration bonds InP onto silicon to combine the strengths of both, while quantum dot lasers offer better temperature stability for uncooled operation. Furthermore, researchers continue to push InP quantum dot structures grown directly on silicon substrates. While these do not remove indium from the equation, they change how much each device needs and how it attaches, reducing consumption. Photonics is widely viewed as one of AI's major bottlenecks. However, the indium phosphide supply chain is itself tightening that bottleneck.

item.title: Nvidia stops AI GPU shipments to Southeast Asia amid purported China cloud access ban, report claims — data centers in Singapore, other countries, in trouble as Commerce Department requires cloud providers to obtain export license
item.description:
AI data centers in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia are facing trouble as Nvidia has reportedly ordered its manufacturing partners to stop shipping AI servers to the region. According to the Financial Times, Dell , Supermicro, and other firms that make AI servers using Nvidia AI GPUs have told their customers from the four countries that the AI chip maker has forbidden them to ship their orders. The move comes as the U.S. closed the loophole that let Chinese AI companies rent compute from data centers outside China equipped with advanced AI chips sourced from American semiconductor manufacturers like Nvidia.

The U.S. has banned the export of advanced AI chips to China since 2022 in an effort to limit its advancement. Even though President Trump eventually allowed Nvidia to export H100 AI GPUs to China in December 2025, companies that wanted to buy them needed to secure an import license from the Commerce Department. Aside from that, the White House is also collecting a 25% fee for every chip, making it more expensive for a data center in China to buy them. Because of this, many Chinese AI labs are instead renting compute from data centers located abroad. They mostly do this in Southeast Asia, which is just around a four-to-six-hour flight from major cities like Hong Kong, Shenzhen, and Shanghai, although some firms are looking in further areas like Europe .

It remains unclear if Nvidia’s order is permanent or temporary, but the new export rules give cloud providers 90 days to apply for an export license and prove that their customers do not include restricted entities. However, one cloud provider executive told the Financial Times that there are no clear instructions on how to go about this. “There’s this new rule but no guidance on execution,” they said. “No one knows how to apply for this license while the 90-day clock is ticking. It’s causing sheer chaos in the region.”

This sudden halt of orders is causing trouble for many data centers in Southeast Asia. Sources say that Aolani, a Singapore-based cloud company with a deal to provide compute to ByteDance, is losing financing for the project as bankers have stopped issuing credit to the tune of $500 million as Nvidia GPU shipments to the region remain in jeopardy. The Chinese social media giant could also potentially drop out of the arrangement, as it won’t be able to access the powerful Nvidia chips that many AI labs still prefer for training their models.

item.title: New delidding tool helps you bake your CPU in the oven to remove heatspreader — Delid-Heat-Mate complements Delid-Die-Mate, reducing mechanical stress on the CPU
item.description:
Thermal Grizzly has just added another product to its list of CPU delidding tools: The Delid-Heat-Mate . After loosening the integrated heat spreader (IHS) with the Delid-Die-Mate, you can use the new "Heat-Mate" to hold your CPU, baking it in the oven to allow the solder to melt, before the CPU falls away under its own weight. The tool is compatible with AMD AM5 and Intel LGA 1700/1851/1954 sockets and only costs $23.28, unlike the Delid-Die-Mate Heater that costs $127.41 and is only compatible with Intel LGA 1851 socket CPUs.

If you’re serious about chasing lower temperatures and higher performance, delidding your CPU and cooling the die directly is one such way to get there. However, delidding is a scary process, with a real risk of chipping your CPU die or prying off small components under the IHS and turning your CPU into a paperweight. Thermal Grizzly has been at the forefront of making that process easier and less risky with its various delidding tools. The Delid-Die-Mate is the first step in this process, exerting a shear force against the IHS and PCB; you could use the delidding tool alone, but using heat is a less mechanically stressful process.

That’s where the Delid-Heat-Mate comes in; it’s a CNC-machined aluminum tool meant to be used after loosening the IHS with a delidding tool. “The CPU is placed in the fixture with the heat spreader facing down and heated in an oven,” Thermal Grizzly states on the Delid-Heat-Mate’s product page. The heat liquefies the indium solder between the IHS and CPU die, and the IHS simply drops under its own weight.

While you still need to buy a Delid-Die-Mate compatible with the type of CPU you have, the Delid-Heat-Mate is compatible with AMD AM5 and Intel LGA 1700/1851/1954 CPUs. In case you don’t have an oven, Thermal Grizzly does have its Delid-Die-Mate Heater V1 , requiring only a 65w USB-C power source — but it’s an add-on for the Delid-Die-Mate V1 for Intel LGA 1851 and costs almost $130.

The Delid-Heat-Mate is a much simpler, more universal, and more affordable option priced under $24 and doing away with any electronics and active heating elements. Your grandmother might have some questions about why you’re baking a block of metal in her oven, though.

item.title: Ukraine downs Russian jet-drone with cheap high-powered laser for the first time — super-fast Shahed knocked out by a 4-kilowatt test system
item.description:
Ukraine has shot down a Russian jet-powered Shahed drone using an air defense laser, reports the Kyiv Independent . This is a first for the 'Blysk' laser system, developed by Ukraine's defense tech company Carmine Sky, and which was deployed on November 19. The news was supported by a Telegram post with embedded video shared by Serhii 'Flash' Beskrestnov, the defense tech advisor to President Zelensky.

See more

Flash explains that the Blysk is currently being tested in active duty to protect an unnamed "critical infrastructure facility" [machine translation of Telegram post content]. Though only in testing for a few days, it seems to have already been a success, as it is the first time a laser has been used to destroy one of the speedy new jet-powered drones Russia has begun to deploy in the conflict.

The 'Geran' drones mentioned by the source publication are Russian adaptations of the Iranian Shahed drones. Russia has used multiple iterations of the Iranian design, dubbed the Geran-2, Geran-5, etc.

Despite the celebratory post highlighting the first jet drone laser kill, Flash was realistic about the technology's potentially slow rollout. "It is still too early to discuss serial production of the laser," wrote the tech advisor on Telegram.

It isn't only Carmine Sky that is working on laser defense tech, noted Flash. This highly complex and capital-intensive battlefield tech is being worked upon by "several companies in Ukraine," it was claimed. We've also seen lasers touted as attractive anti-drone solutions by other nations.

Even if they might be expensive to develop, lasers are often praised for their low cost per shot. Blysk reportedly has a power output of 4kW, and using a shot of energy of this magnitude is far cheaper than firing a missile, for example. We've seen it claimed that the UK's DragonFire laser weapon costs roughly £10 ($13) per shot in energy consumption, and the Blysk cost per shot is probably in the same ballpark.

The source report says that weather hasn't been ideal for laser defenses recently, with "persistent cloud cover and fog." Unlike missiles and bullets, common weather phenomena like cloud cover can seriously weaken a laser beam before it reaches its target. Lasers will likely therefore never replace kinetic forms of air defense, but will be deployed to augment existing protections.

item.title: New York Governor Kathy Hochul signs ban on AI chatbot toys backed by $15,000 daily fines — takes effect in 90 days after holiday rush
item.description:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has signed a bill that effectively bans the sale of toys with built-in AI chatbots within the state over concerns about what they might say to kids. But the ban will come too late for this Holiday season, leaving parents at risk of buying toys without realizing the risks that they could pose to their children. The ban will come into effect 90 days from Tuesday, November 24, WXXI News reports , and targets toys like stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that use a microphone and speaker to allow children to communicate with a relatively rudimentary chatbot. But with safeguards often lacking, it can be difficult to predict how these toys will behave and what they will say to young children who might not realize what they are speaking to.

New York's ban comes after similar moves by other states around the United States, with California already announcing a four-year moratorium on the sale and manufacturing of AI toys to children under 16. Pennsylvania is also considering similar action. Back in New York, Hochul has hinted that more AI safety proposals are in the works for 2027. “We'll set clear safety standards and put independent experts inside these companies to make sure that they're following the rules, and that we'll insist that humans remain in control, and with plans to contain the danger if something does go wrong,” the governor said. There are a few ways that could happen, with State Senator Andrew Gournardes (D-Brooklyn) noting that a new Common Sense Media Your AI Safety Institute report found AI chatbot toys can undermine a child's relationships with their family and friends.

The ban will hit toy manufacturers, sellers, and operators with fines of $15,000 per day if they are found in violation. It also follows similar tech-focused child safety laws, such as requiring age verification for social media for anyone under the age of 18. Warning labels must also be present. It's possible that Hochul will look to expand that requirement to AI chatbots, including those not built into toys.

Alarm over AI chatbots is nothing new, of course, but the new wave of devices aimed at children is causing concern. Beyond the impact on children, AI psychosis continues to be an issue, with a June 2025 report finding that OpenAI's ChatGPT encouraged dangerous and untrue beliefs about a range of things, including trying to convince one user that they were Neo from the popular The Matrix movie franchise. Some companies have worked to make their products safer, with limited success. OpenAI released a new version of its ChatGPT chatbot that would be less sycophantic and push back against users more, only for those users to revolt over the move . OpenAI later rolled the change back.
